In the cancer prevention and post-diagnosis settings in turn, we first review the epidemiological evidence linking exercise with primary cancer risk and disease outcomes after diagnosis. We then summarize data from key clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of structured exercise therapy on clinical end points and on blood-based and tissue-based biomarkers in individuals with or at risk of cancer. Modification of an individual’s exposure to exercise can alter the host macroenvironment, leading to changes in distant tissue and/or tumour microenvironments. Such adaptations might alter the efficacy of conventional cancer therapies, and the newest developments in this rapidly expanding field are also reviewed herein. Finally, we outline a translational framework to facilitate continued development of exercise as an anticancer therapeutic modality and a path towards precision exercise oncology.

title: Right-sizing treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer: evolving algorithms across the disease continuum
abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast cancer has undergone one of the most profound therapeutic transformations in oncology. Once associated with poor outcomes, it is now a highly curable disease in the early-stage setting, and a substantial proportion of patients with metastatic disease survive beyond 5 years. This progress reflects the development of multiple HER2-targeted therapies, including monoclonal antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates and tyrosine-kinase inhibitors. Most notably, the HER2-targeted antibody–drug conjugate trastuzumab deruxtecan has rapidly been moved into earlier lines of therapy, with emerging roles in the first-line metastatic setting, adjuvant treatment of high-risk residual disease and neoadjuvant therapy. This expansion creates new opportunities, but also crucial evidence gaps regarding optimal sequencing, retreatment and selection of patients for treatment intensification. As treatment options expand, the central challenge is to right-size therapy across the disease continuum, which is the focus of this Review. In patients with early-stage disease, this right-sizing involves carefully de-intensifying treatment for those with low-risk tumours, optimizing neoadjuvant chemotherapy backbones and escalating therapy for those with residual disease; in patients with advanced-stage disease, it requires optimizing maintenance treatment strategies (for example, using palbociclib or tucatinib) after induction therapy, while integrating these maintenance regimens with the novel option of first-line trastuzumab deruxtecan plus pertuzumab, for which the optimal treatment duration and subsequent sequencing remain uncertain. Tissue, plasma and dynamic imaging-based biomarkers are beginning to inform this process, with several showing promising potential for clinical implementation.

title: Adjuvant radiotherapy improves outcomes in patients with completely resected atypical meningioma
A modular framework for antibody–drug conjugate biomarkers
abstract: The availability of approved antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) has rapidly expanded across oncology indications, yet biomarker development remains dominated by semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry. Robust biomarkers are needed to improve patient selection, guide therapeutic sequencing and identify resistance mechanisms that inform rational combinations. ADC activity depends on target antigen expression, linker chemistry and payload characteristics all within the context of the tumour microenvironment. Consequently, treatment response cannot be predicted solely by target expression. A more comprehensive biomarker framework is required that accounts for antigen abundance and accessibility, intracellular trafficking and linker cleavage, and tumour susceptibility to the payload. Furthermore, biomarkers of toxicity have been largely overlooked, even though toxicity can be equally determinant of clinical utility. In this Review, we outline a modular framework for ADC biomarker development organized around these components. We distinguish established evidence from emerging strategies and discuss technologies that could enable assessment of these determinants. We consider how modular biomarkers might inform patient selection, therapeutic sequencing, rational combinations, dose optimization and regulatory strategy while highlighting the various challenges that must be addressed before broad clinical adoption. Harmonized development across trials, tumour types and geographical regions will be essential to move biomarker development beyond empirical target-expression thresholds.

title: An imprecise label in the era of precision medicine: labelling and access for daraxonrasib, the first pan-RAS inhibitor approval
abstract: The FDA recently approved daraxonrasib for patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who received at least one prior systemic therapy or who are not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy. Critics call the second clause non-evidence based. However, this imprecision enables access: trials generally enrol only patients with good performance status, which does not reflect the realities for most patients with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who never reach second-line therapy because their clinical condition deteriorates first. Real-world evidence should resolve any remaining uncertainty.

title: No cancer research without older adults, from prevention to end of life: a manifesto
abstract: Older adults (aged ≥65 years) comprise the majority of people diagnosed with cancer, yet they remain proportionally underrepresented in cancer research at every stage of the pathway. We call on funders, regulators, researchers and journals to make systematic inclusion of older adults the norm, across studies spanning from cancer prevention to end-of-life care.

title: Combining locoregional treatments and immunotherapies in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: The systemic treatment landscape of unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma has been transformed by immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens. These advances have led to efforts to combine ICIs with locoregional therapies (LRTs), particularly transarterial chemoembolization, transarterial radioembolization and external beam radiotherapy, in an attempt to improve tumour control and extend the benefits of ICIs to patients with intermediate-stage disease. The rationale for this combination approach is provided by the ability of LRTs to induce immunogenic cell death and tumour antigen release and to reprogramme the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. Five phase III trials have thus far shown improvements in progression-free survival and objective response rates with regimens combining ICIs with transarterial chemoembolization. Early-phase and real-world data also support the combination of ICIs with transarterial radioembolization or external beam radiotherapy, particularly in selected patients with focal disease unsuitable for embolization or portal vein tumour thrombosis. However, various challenges remain, including patient selection and therapy sequencing, response assessment, and the growing difficulties in demonstrating survival advantages in the context of widespread post-progression crossover and effective subsequent therapies. In this Review, we describe the biological rationale, summarize the clinical evidence and discuss future directions for trial design, imaging and biomarker-driven patient selection in the integration of LRTs with immune-based regimens for patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Problematic control arms in National Cancer Institute myeloma trials
abstract: Three of five National Cancer Institute-sponsored randomized trials that are currently enrolling patients with multiple myeloma have control arms that no longer reflect the standard of care, despite two of these trials being activated in 2026. Comparators in federally sponsored trials need reassessment and, if necessary, updating to reflect changes in clinical practice before and during enrolment.
